title: Sorted Squares From Both Ends
statement:
You get an array nums sorted in non-decreasing order. It may contain negative numbers.

Square every number and return the squares as a new array, also in non-decreasing order. Aim for O(n), without sorting again.

examples.why: -6 is the smallest number but its square, 36, is the largest. Squaring in place breaks the order on the negative side.
All negative: the squares come out in exactly the reverse order.
Equal squares from both signs must all be kept.

constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Squaring and then sorting works in O(n log n). Where in the input do the largest squares live?
The largest square is at one of the two ends: either the most negative number or the most positive one.
Put a pointer on each end. Compare the two squares, write the bigger one into the last free slot of the output, and move that pointer inward.

explain.intuition:
Squares are large at both ends of a sorted array and small in the middle, near zero. So the input, once squared, is a valley: decreasing then increasing. You do not know where the bottom is, but you always know where the top is: at the left end or the right end.

So fill the output from the back. Compare the squares at both ends, place the bigger one in the last open slot, and step that end inward. It is the merge step of merge sort, run on two halves that are both sorted from the outside in.
steps: Create an output array of the same length. Set lo = 0, hi = n − 1, and write = n − 1.
Write the bigger one to out[write] and move that pointer inward (lo++ or hi--).
Decrease write and repeat. Return the output.
pitfalls: Using lo < hi as the loop condition, which skips the last remaining element.
Filling from the front: the smallest square is somewhere in the middle, not at an end.
Sorting the squares with the default JavaScript sort(), which compares numbers as strings (100 comes before 9).

solutions.title: Square, then sort
solutions.idea: Square every element and sort the result numerically.

solutions.title: Two pointers, fill from the back
solutions.idea: The largest remaining square is always at one of the two ends, so place it last and move inward.

followups: Apply any function f(x) = a·x² + b·x + c instead of squaring and still return sorted output in O(n). How does the sign of a change the fill direction?
Return only the k smallest squares. Can you start in the middle instead?
